"We need diversity of thought in the world to face the new challenges" - Tim Bernard-lee

In recent years there has been a Cambrian explosion of new models created, each claiming to be State of the Art (SOTA). As you may know by now, there is no single modelling approach that is perfect (<https://openreview.net/pdf?id=wEc1mgAjU->), and with so many different approaches it is difficult to stay on top of them all.

While it can take a substantial to keep afloat of all the models, we can classify most networks into families, which gives us an intuitive starting point for understanding how a network may attempt to model our data. This chapter discusses a number of neural network families, and briefly looks at a selection of models from these families that we cannot cover in full detail. We will apply our selected models on data from the M5 competition (all this code will be available in the accompanying notebook in the GitHub repository).  

In this chapter, we will:

- Cover neural network families used in forecasting
- Discuss the fundamentals underpinning these families
- Brief over some specific neural architectures within each family
- Demonstrate how to utilise Nixtla's NeuralForecast to run specific networks

## Setting up our M5 dataset

We use the M5 dataset in this chapter. For more background about this dataset, you can refer to the M5 competition in Chapter 1 and the exploration of the dataset in Chapter 2. In this section, we will load the dataset and perform some basic analysis.

### Configuring our dataset

First, the related imports and configurations. We place the dataset inside a folder called "data" alongside the script/notebook where our code runs.

```{python}
#| label: chapter-10-setup
#| message: false
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path

custom_palette = ["#000000", "#0072B2", "#D55E00","#009E73","#CC79A7", "#56B4E9","#E69F00"]


class CFG:
    data_folder = Path.cwd().parent / "data"
    img_dim1 = 12
    img_dim2 = 6
    fontsize = 18

plt.rcParams.update({'figure.figsize': (CFG.img_dim1,CFG.img_dim2)}) 
```

### Loading and preprocessing the data

To explore the dataset, we need to load it and convert it into a pandas dataframe. We build a function to achieve this.

```{python}
#| label: load-m5-subset
def load_m5_subset(data_folder: Path) -> pd.DataFrame:

    # Construct filepath
    filepath = data_folder / 'M5_t20_ABC.csv'
    
    # Verify file exists
    if not filepath.exists():
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"Data file not found at {filepath}")
        
    # Read data
    df = pd.read_csv(filepath, index_col=0)
    
    # Convert date to datetime
    df['date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['date'])
    
    # Remove last 28 days of each series
    df_sorted = df.sort_values(['item_id', 'date'])
    def remove_tail_values(group):
        return group.iloc[:-28]
    df = df_sorted.groupby('item_id', group_keys=False).apply(remove_tail_values).reset_index(drop=True)
    
    # Add time-based features
    df['year'] = df['date'].dt.year
    df['month'] = df['date'].dt.month
    df['dayofweek'] = df['date'].dt.dayofweek
    df['quarter'] = df['date'].dt.quarter
    df['week_of_year'] = df['date'].dt.isocalendar().week
    return df
```

### Summarizing the dataset

We also need to get some basic statistics of the dataset. We use the following function to compute the summary statistics of the M5 competition dataset.

```{python}
#| label: analyze-dataset
def analyze_dataset(df: pd.DataFrame) -> dict:
    # Get ABC distribution by unique products
    abc_dist = df.groupby('item_id')['ABC_class'].first().value_counts().to_dict()
    
    analysis = {
        'n_series': df['item_id'].nunique(),
        'n_stores': df['state_id'].nunique(),
        'date_range': (df['date'].min(), df['date'].max()),
        'total_sales': df['sold'].sum(),
        'mean_price': df['sell_price'].mean(),
        'abc_distribution': abc_dist,
        'sales_by_class': df.groupby('ABC_class')['sold'].sum().to_dict(),
        'avg_price_by_class': df.groupby('ABC_class')['sell_price'].mean().to_dict()
    }
    
    return analysis
```

### Visualizing patterns

And finally, we need to build a function to plot out some examples of the sales data.

```{python}
#| label: plot-sales-analysis
def plot_sales_analysis(series: pd.DataFrame, figsize=(15, 10)):
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=figsize)
    
    # Sales over time
    axes[0].plot(series['date'], series['sold'], color = custom_palette[1], alpha=0.7)
    axes[0].set_title(f"Sales Over Time for {series['item_id'].iloc[0]}")
    axes[0].set_xlabel('Date')
    axes[0].set_ylabel('Units Sold')
    
    # Sales by day of week
    sns.boxplot(data=series, x='dayofweek', y='sold', ax=axes[1], color = custom_palette[2])
    axes[1].set_title('Sales Distribution by Day of Week')
    axes[1].set_xlabel('Day of Week')
    axes[1].set_ylabel('Units Sold')
    
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
    
    # Print summary statistics
    print(
        "\nSummary Statistics: "
        f"{series['sold'].describe()}"
    )
```

### Modeling a subset of the data

To be able to investigate multiple models quickly, we create a small subset of time series taken from the M5 competition, from `locn_id` (location) CA. Let's quickly load this data...

```{python}
#| label: load-data
df = load_m5_subset(CFG.data_folder)

# Analyze dataset
analysis = analyze_dataset(df)
analysis
```

A quick analysis of our data shows we have 60 unique items, tracked over 5.5 years (January 2011 until June 2016). The items are evenly split across the ABC classification, with 20 products in each group. 'A' items are high-volume products that make up about 80% of total sales (1.46 million out of 1.82 million units). 'B' items are medium-volume and account for around 15% (272,000 units), while 'C' items are low-volume and make up the remaining 5% (87,000 units). This kind of difference in sales volume is normal, but in this case, we created the distribution on purpose. In the original data, you'd see something like: A = 15%, B = 25%, and C = 60% of items. We can also see a clear trend between sales volume and pricing --- high-volume 'A' items tend to be cheaper (averaging $1.74), while low-volume 'C' items are more expensive (averaging $3.62).

### Exploring variation in different time series

Let's plot out some series to investigate some of the patterns in our dataset.

```{python}
# Select series to plot
series_to_plot = ['FOODS_3_090', 'FOODS_3_714', 'HOUSEHOLD_2_437', 'HOUSEHOLD_1_448']

# Create figure with subplots

for idx, (series_id, ax) in enumerate(zip(series_to_plot, axes)):

    series = series.sort_values('date')
    
    # Get last 36 months
```

Looking at a few individual time series, we can see some variation. The first item (FOOD_3_090) which we have seen earlier, has a high magnitude of sales but has several data drop offs. There are several such instances in the dataset, and it is unlikely that we can model these sets perfectly without significant data wrangling and feature engineering. The rest of the time series mostly show straightforward patterns, ranging from high to low volume selling items.

As our goal here is to discuss and demonstrate modelling with different architectures, we are not going to do too much data wrangling but simply model all items in the subset. We will first need to set up our data quickly for modelling with `neuralforecast`, we'll attempt to model the last 90 days of each series to get an idea of how they perform on a typical demand dataset. Neuralforecast requires a specific format of the dataset, in our Jupyter notebook for chapter 10 on GitHub, you will find the details of how we setup the datasets. Just be aware that, this could be done better with more hyper parameter tuning, and different data sets will see different results.       

## Exploring some neural network families

While there is an ever increasing number of neural architectural designs, most are designs are variations stemming from general structures, which we can refer to as a family. Having some understanding of each neural network families can be useful when encountering new models. These can largely be broken down into: Multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs, which we have already discussed), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN), Gated Neural Networks, Transformers, Foundation Models (for example LLMs; which Karpathy suggests are best called Autoregressive Transformers), and latest family at time or writing, Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN). There are also hybridised architectures that mix together elements of different networks. In this chapter we will use Nixtla's Neuralforecast, which covers many neural network families and the most popular network designs within them, as you can see in the table. 

The full table of models and their capabilities (including univariate/multivariate support and forecast type) can be found in the [Nixtla NeuralForecast documentation](https://nixtlaverse.nixtla.io/neuralforecast/docs/capabilities/overview.html). ## MLP

Multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) are generally considered a misnomer. As we discussed earlier this is more to do with the origin of neural networks which initially used activation functions like sigmoid and tanh before alternatives became common.

Generally, MLP refers to networks with that feed-forward (FFNs). So, by this standard CNNs are technically as MLPs, although we consider them a separate family. As we used MLPs/FFNs to discuss the fundamentals of *deep learning* in chapters 4 to 6, we will not be discussing them in great detail here.

You usually see MLPs/FFNs used directly, such as the MLP and MLPMultivariate models in `neuralforecast`. However, FFNs can be used in various ways to i.e. restricted outputs such as DeepNPTS, or to combine information from other *blocks* of a network together i.e. SOFTS.

In @tbl-nixtla-nf-model-table we presented these four models, MLP, MLPMultivariate, DeepNPTS, and SOFTS. These are considered true MLP-based models. Let's look at these in depth here:

* MLP - This is a straightforward MLP model using tahn or relu activation functions. 
* MLPMultivariate - MLP adapted for multivariate modelling
* DeepNPTS - Is non-parametric (distribution free). This approach uses the neural network (NN) to learn sampling probabilities over the observed inputs. It makes predictions by sampling from the past values, not creating new values, which can be useful.    
* SOFTS (Series-cOre Fused Time Series forecaster) - Models multivariate time-series, by attempting to balance signals in independent channels while accounting for cross-channel interactions through a centralised architecture, instead of using an attention mechanism discussed in the Transformer chapter, that is compares every channel with every other channel. SOFTS aggregates information into a global 'core' representation, then fuses this to individual channel data. In theory this approach might help in forecasting data in panels like traffic networks, energy grids, or retail sales across multiple stores, where attention-based models might be computationally expensive or prone to over-fitting noisy channel relationships. 

### MLP Hybrids

While the previous architectures directly use MLPs/FFNs networks, there are several popular methods that are classified under the MLP family, due to these structures using MLPs as the base blocks for underpinning these networks. Several of these networks are hybrids that are specialised for time-series forecasting.

* NBEATS/NBEATSx - This is a specialised architecture that uses MLP blocks within a broader architectural framework. It combines backward and forward residual links with specialized blocks for trend and seasonality.
* NHITS - Similar to NBEATS, it's a hybrid architecture that extends NBEATS with interpolation and pooling.
* TiDE (Time-series Dense Encoder): While using MLP components, it's more accurately described as a transformer-inspired architecture without the attention mechanism. It uses time embeddings and specialized layers.
* TimeMixer/TSMixer/TSMixerx: These are actually MLP-Mixer inspired architectures, adapting the transformer-like mixing concept but using MLPs instead of attention. They're closer to transformer variants than traditional MLPs.
* NLinear: This is a linear model with neural components, not a traditional MLP.

We will cover two of these in the following sections.

#### N-BEATS

N-BEATS (Neural Basis Expansion Analysis for Interpretable Time Series) was perhaps the first pure deep learning approach to surpass statistical modelling approaches, as was famously established on M4 competition data in the original paper @oreshkinNBEATSNeuralBasis2020. It outperformed the competition winning entry (an ES-RNN) by 3%. N-BEATS achieved this by using *neural basis expansion* to augment *target ($y$)* data, by projecting it with *basis functions*, which allowed the model to learn non-linear relationships. You may wonder what is *basis functions* are, and why do they help? Let's use a classic example - if we were attempting to predict ice cream sales based on temperature a simple model might appear linear (as below).

```{python}
#| label: nbeats-linear-example
# Generate example data
temp = np.array([14, 16, 18, 20, 22, 24, 26, 28, 30]).reshape((-1, 1))  
sales = np.array([50, 55, 60, 80, 110, 160, 180, 190, 200])  

# Linear regression
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
model = LinearRegression()
model.fit(temp, sales)

plt.scatter(temp, sales, color=custom_palette[0])
plt.plot(temp, model.predict(temp), color=custom_palette[1])
plt.xlabel('Temperature')
plt.ylabel('Sales')
plt.tight_layout(pad=3.0)
plt.show()
```

Despite the linear function performing OK, we can see that the relationship isn't so simple. Sales increase slowly at first, then rapidly as temperature rises. Clearly a linear model is too simple, a non-linear model would be better. This is where *basis expansion* comes into play, by applying polynomial terms up to the third degree, we can expand our *basis*, allowing our model to learn both quadratic and cubic non-linear relationships.

```{python}
#| label: nbeats-polynomial-example
# Polynomial basis expansion
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures

poly = PolynomialFeatures(degree=3, include_bias=False)
temp_poly = poly.fit_transform(temp)

model = LinearRegression()
model.fit(temp_poly, sales)

plt.scatter(temp, sales, color=custom_palette[0])
plt.plot(temp, model.predict(temp_poly), color=custom_palette[1])
plt.xlabel('Temperature')
plt.ylabel('Sales')
plt.show()
```

There are many different basis expansions, such as logarithms, piecewise-linear splines, binning, natural cubic splines, and squares, but these are restrictive. We can create customised basis expansions. As the precise basis expansion is unknown to us, it is often better to learn it from our data. This is exactly what *neural basis expansion* in N-BEATS attempts to do; automatically select and optimize for the best basis expansion.

The precise architecture of N-BEATS is as follows: 

![The N-BEATS architecture; From B. N. Oreshkin, D. Carpov, N. Chapados, and Y. Bengio, “N-BEATS: Neural basis expansion analysis for interpretable time series forecasting,” arXiv [cs.LG], May 24, 2019. Available: http://arxiv.org/abs/1905.10437. [Accessed: Jan. 18, 2025]](images/chap10_images/nbeats_architecture.png){fig-align="centre" fig-alt="The N-BEATS architecture showing stacks, blocks, and residual connections"}

This diagram shows that N-BEATS processes time series data by first splitting it into lookback and forecast periods. The length of the lookback window is important for capturing relevant patterns - originally the authors of N-BEATS used 2x forecast horizon for generic architecture, and up to 7x for interpretable versions, see @oreshkinNBEATSNeuralBasis2020. However, the optimal lookback length depends on your data's seasonality structure. We represent this input sequence of historical values as $x = [x_1, ..., x_s]$.

The yellow rectangle, of the architecture, shows that N-BEATS employs a hierarchical structure of stacks (orange rectangles), each stack specializes in modeling specific time series components like trend or seasonality.  While it is useful to think like this, typically the stacks operate on the same input (lookback period), with the outputs of each stack being summed to produce a final forecast. The strength of this approach comes from allowing each stack to learn different aspects of an underlying data generating process. 

Each block (detailed in the blue rectangle) implements a novel dual-output architecture. The network splits into two branches that simultaneously produce: 

1. A backcast that attempts to reconstruct the input data, and
2. a partial forecast of future values, which is mathematically represented as: 
   $$\text{Block}(x) = (b(x), f(x)),$$
   where $b(x)$ is the backcast and $f(x)$ the forecast.

Within each block, a fully connected neural network with four layers learns expansion coefficients $θ$. These are then combined with basis functions $g(t)$ through neural basis expansion. 
For interpretable trend modeling:

$$g_{\text{trend}}(t) = [1, t, t^2, ..., t^p]$$

And for seasonal patterns with period T:

$$g_{\text{seasonal}}(t) = [\sin(2\pi t/T), \cos(2\pi t/T), ..., \sin(2\pi ht/T), \cos(2\pi ht/T)]$$

Blocks connect through residual links within each stack - which allows each block to focus on modeling residual patterns not captured by previous blocks. The stack aggregates partial forecasts from its blocks through summation, and the final forecast combines outputs across all stacks. 

This residual stacking is what enables N-BEATS to decompose time series, somewhat similarly to traditional statistical approaches like ARIMA. The primary difference is that ARIMA focuses on quality of the residuals, and needs manual adjustments based on the domain knowledge, while N-BEATS utilises more powerful basis functions thus more expressive. N-BEATS interpretable variant enforces specific basis functions - polynomial for trend and Fourier for seasonality - enabling clear component decomposition.

N-BEATSx extends this architecture by incorporating exogenous variables $X$ alongside a target variable $y$. N-BEATS processes only historical target values $y$ₜ through its blocks, N-BEATSx processes a covariate matrix $X$ containing external features @olivaresNeuralBasisExpansion2023. For example, we could include variables like price and calendar features, or any other relevant external data. The core architectural elements - stacks, blocks, and residual connections - remain the same, but each block in N-BEATSx learns from both the target and exogenous variables. Allowing N-BEATSx to capture relationships between the target and external influences, along with time variating patterns. Of course, adding exogenous variables is not guaranteed to improve performance. 

#### N-HITS

In 2022, N-HiTS (Neural Hierarchical Interpolation for Time Series) improved upon N-BEATS by addressing two limitations for long forecast horizons: decreasing accuracy, and computational cost as forecast horizons increase in length. It maintains the core neural basis expansion concept of N-BEATS, while introducing two changes: multi-rate data sampling and hierarchical interpolation @challuNHiTSNeuralHierarchical2022.

Multi-rate data sampling, occurs at block level through *MaxPool* layers. Each stack's blocks apply MaxPool with a specified kernel size to smooth input signal. That allows each stack to look at a series at different scales.

```{python}
#| label: nhits-maxpool-example
# Original data
data = np.array([3, 6, 4, 0, 8, 5, 3, 2, 7, 9, 6, 0, 5, 3, 2])
x = np.arange(len(data))

# Function to perform max pooling
def max_pool(data, kernel_size):
    output = []
    for i in range(0, len(data), kernel_size):
        end = min(i + kernel_size, len(data))
        output.append(np.max(data[i:end]))
    return np.array(output)

# Calculate pooled data
pool_3 = max_pool(data, 3)
pool_5 = max_pool(data, 5)

# Create x values for pooled data (centered in their windows)
x_pool_3 = np.arange(1, len(pool_3) * 3, 3)[0:len(pool_3)]
x_pool_5 = np.arange(2, len(pool_5) * 5, 5)[0:len(pool_5)]

# Create the plots
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(12, 7))

# Top plot - data with alternating kernel=3 bands
ax1.plot(x, data, 'o-', color=custom_palette[0], linewidth=1.5, markersize=6, zorder=5)

colours_k3 = [custom_palette[1], custom_palette[5]]
for idx, i in enumerate(range(0, len(data), 3)):
    end = min(i + 3, len(data)) - 1
    ax1.axvspan(i - 0.5, end + 0.5, alpha=0.15, color=colours_k3[idx % 2],
                label='Kernel Size 3 windows' if idx == 0 else None)

# Horizontal bars for kernel=5 at the top
bar_y = 9.8
for idx, i in enumerate(range(0, len(data), 5)):
    end = min(i + 5, len(data)) - 1
    ax1.plot([i, end], [bar_y, bar_y], color=custom_palette[6], linewidth=4, solid_capstyle='butt',
             label='Kernel Size 5 windows' if idx == 0 else None)
    ax1.plot([i, i], [bar_y - 0.3, bar_y + 0.3], color=custom_palette[6], linewidth=2)
    ax1.plot([end, end], [bar_y - 0.3, bar_y + 0.3], color=custom_palette[6], linewidth=2)

ax1.set_ylim(-0.5, 10.5)
ax1.set_title('Original Time Series with Pooling Windows')
ax1.legend(loc='upper right', fontsize=11, framealpha=0.9)

# Bottom plot - pooled results
ax2.plot(x_pool_3, pool_3, 'o-', label='Kernel Size 3', color=custom_palette[1], linewidth=2)
ax2.plot(x_pool_5, pool_5, 'o-', label='Kernel Size 5', color=custom_palette[6], linewidth=2)
ax2.legend(loc='upper right', fontsize=11)
ax2.set_title('Max Pooled Results')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Larger kernel sizes create stronger smoothing, emphasising long-term patterns, while smaller sizes preserve short-term details. N-HiTS uses a top-down approach where initial stacks focus on long-term effects (larger kernels) and later stacks capture short-term patterns (smaller kernels).

Hierarchical interpolation, reduces computational load by allowing stacks to forecast at different time scales. This is controlled by an expressiveness ratio that determines how many predictions each stack makes within the forecast horizon. For example, with a ratio of 1/2, a stack predicts every second value of a final forecast:

$$\mathrm{predictions}_{\mathrm{stack}} = \mathrm{horizon_length} * \mathrm{expressiveness\_ratio}.$$

The final prediction combines interpolated forecasts from all stacks:

$$\hat{y} = \sum_{s=1}^S \mathrm{interpolate}(\hat{y}_s, \mathrm{horizon\_length}),$$

where $\hat{y}_s$ is the forecast from stacks, and interpolate() upsamples the prediction to match the forecast horizon length.

As a result of this, N-HiTS allows earlier stacks to focus on weekly patterns with fewer predictions, while later stacks handle daily or hourly patterns with higher resolution. The expressiveness ratio typically increases exponentially between stacks or aligns with known cyclical patterns in the data. All of this helps N-HiTS models to be more efficient and accurate for predicting long horizons.


## CNN

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are widely used networks for computer vision, that saw an adaption in 2018 to allow them to work with on time series forecasting @baiEmpiricalEvaluationGeneric2018. Bai et al's (2018) demonstrated that CNNs can outperform tradition sequential networks, such as RNNs, while avoiding issues with; exploding/vanishing gradient, and memory retention. Along with the advantage of computational efficiency due to parallel computation of outputs. Their Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) architecture, was a promising start to using CNNs for forecasting. While CNNs are not currently the most popular family for forecasting, architectures like BiTCN, TCN and TimesNet (particularly TCN) have shown promising results.  

CNNs processes three-dimensional tensors, with 1D CNNs operate on input shape (batch_size, input_length, input_size) and output shape (batch_size, input_length, output_size). For forecasting, input_size represents features at each timestep, output_size for predicted variables.

From the input tensor (batch_size, input_length, input_size), kernels operate along the temporal dimension (input_length). Kernels are learnable weight matrices that moves across the sequence of input data, processing fixed-size windows of data. For a single-channel input, a kernel of size k examines k consecutive timesteps, element-wise multiplying its weights with these values and summing the results. When processing multi-channel inputs (like temperature, price, volume), the kernel becomes a 2D matrix of shape (kernel_size × input_channels), performing calculations across all channels simultaneously to capture cross-feature relationships.

![CNN Kernel and MultiChannel diagram](images/chap10_images/CNN_kernals.png){fig-align="centre" fig-alt="Diagram showing how CNN kernels operate on single and multi-channel time series inputs"}

Kernels slide across squences according to stride length, typically we would want `stride=1` to avoid skipped timesteps. erform weighted sums across $k$ timesteps. Each kernel of size $k$ performs a weighted sum across $k$ timesteps. For example, with kernel $[0.5, 0.3, 0.2]$ and sales data $[100, 120, 80]$, the operation computes $(0.5×100 + 0.3×120 + 0.2×80) = 106$. Multiple kernels operate in parallel, each learning different temporal patterns, with their count determining the layer's output_channels. Each layer uses multiple parallel kernels ($kernel_size × input_channels × output_channels$) to learn temporal patterns.

Causality in sequence prediction requires that each output depends only on current and previous inputs in the sequence, never future ones. This is achieved through left-side zero padding, where zeros are added only to the start of the sequence. For a kernel size $k$ and dilation rate $d$, we add $p = (k-1) × d$ zeros to the left side. This asymmetric padding ensures the kernel's window never sees future values while maintaining the desired output length. 

In multi-channel inputs (when using exogenous variable), kernels extend across all input channels, with dimensions ($kernel_size × input_channels × output_channels$), enabling the network to learn cross-feature relationships.

![CNN receptive field growth diagram](images/chap10_images/CNN_receptive_field_growth.png){fig-align="centre" fig-alt="Diagram showing how receptive field grows with network depth and dilation"}


A receptive field - span of input positions that influence each output - grows with network depth according to $r = 1 + Σ(k-1)$ for $n$ layers with kernel size $k$. This basic formulation can be enhanced through dilation, where kernels skip $d-1$ inputs between elements, effectively expanding the field without increasing parameters. The dilated receptive field becomes $r = 1 + Σ(k-1)d^i$, where $d$ is the dilation rate and $i$ is the layer index.

To prevent 'holes' in a receptive field - gaps where certain inputs fail to influence an output - the kernel size $k$ must exceed dilation base $b$. Consider a six-timestep sequence with kernel size 2 and dilation base 3: the model would see timesteps $[t, t-3, t-6]$ while completely missing $[t-1, t-2, t-4, t-5]$. These holes create blind spots in the network's view of the input sequence, severely impacting model performance. For a sequence of length $l$, the minimum required layers for full coverage (without holes) is: $n = ⌈log_k(l(k-1) + 1)⌉$.

For forecasting specifically, input and target sequences are created through a sliding windows approach. Given a forecast horizon h, each input sequence generates a target sequence shifted h steps forward. The maximum forecast horizon is limited by output_length, with window stride controlling training sample overlap.

CNNs and RNNs handle memory requirements differently across training and inference phases. During training, CNN memory usage scales with sequence length, batch size, and number of parameters (kernel_size × input_channels × output_channels per layer). During inference, RNNs maintain only their hidden state, while CNNs require the complete effective history of inputs, creating a memory-speed tradeoff.

These architectural principles - causality, dense predictions (stride=1), and dilated convolutions - form the foundation for advanced models like TCNs. When adapting models between domains with different memory requirements, careful adjustment of kernel size (k) and dilation rate (d) is crucial for maintaining performance while managing computational resources.


## Graph Neural Networks

In the sales data we analyzed in the beginning of this chapter, forecasting the sales of all the goods requires a model to capture the inter-series relationships, e.g., people buy more party items during the weekend, and the intra-series relationships, e.g., people grabbing a pizza might also buy a cola. Many statistical time series forecasting models already atempts to capture such relations, for example, vector autoregressive (VAR) models. Graph neural networks (GNN) is a good candidate for such multivariate forecasting tasks because they model the interactions between series using a more generic concept: graph.

A graph describes relationships between objects. For example, we can use the following to describe the idea that people buy pizza together with cola and salad:

![Pizza, Cola, and Salad graph](images/chap10_images/graph_concepts.png){#fig-graph-concept width=50%}

In @fig-graph-concept, the circles "Pizza", "Salad", and "Cola" are the vertices, the lines connecting them are the so-called edges. The same information can be described using a matrix, where the elements of it are 1 if there is an edge between the corresponding vertices, e.g., Pizza-Salad, and 0 otherwise, e.g., Salad and Cola. This matrix is called the adjacency matrix, which looks like this for our pizza-salad-cola example:

$$
\mathbf A = \begin{pmatrix}
0 & 1 & 1 \\
1 & 0 & 0 \\
1 & 0 & 0
\end{pmatrix}.
$${#eq-gnn-graph-adjacency}

The first row in @eq-gnn-graph-adjacency is for "Pizza", the second for "Salad", and the third for "Cola". 

GNN models operates on such graph structures. To demonstrate how it works, we discuss one of the most intuitive GNN strategies called message passing. First of all, we have a representation of each vertex which is usually a embedding tensor, $\mathbf h$.

![Representations of Pizza, Salad, and Cola.](images/chap10_images/graph-node-representations.png){#fig-graph-vertex-representation width=60%}

The idea is simple: each vertex aggregates all the information from its neighbors and combines with the information itself carries. In the Pizza-Salad-Cola example, the "Pizza" vertex will aggregate the information from "Salad" and "Cola" vertices, and then combine with its own information. For example, we update the representation of "Pizza" as follows:

1. Aggregate the information from "Salad" and "Cola" vertices: 

   $$
   \mathbf m_P = \mathbf h_{\text{Salad}} + \mathbf h_{\text{Cola}}
   = \begin{pmatrix} 1.0 \\ 0.5 \\ 1.5 \\ 2.5 \\ 1.5 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 1.5 \\ 1.0 \\ 0.5 \\ 3.0 \\ 0.5 \end{pmatrix}.
   $$
2. Combine the aggregated information with the information of "Pizza" itself:

   $$
    \begin{align}
    \mathbf h_{\text{Pizza}} &= \sigma\left(
        \mathbf W_{\text{self}} \cdot \mathbf h_{\text{Pizza}} + \mathbf W_{\text{neighbor}} \cdot \mathbf m_P
    \right) \\
    &= \sigma\left(
        \mathbf W_{\text{self}} \cdot \begin{pmatrix}
        0.5 \\ 2.0 \\ 1.5 \\ 0.55 \\ 1.0
        \end{pmatrix}
        + 
        \mathbf W_{\text{neighbor}}  \cdot \left( 
        \begin{pmatrix} 1.0 \\ 0.5 \\ 1.5 \\ 2.5 \\ 1.5 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 1.0 \\ 0.5 \\ 1.5 \\ 2.5 \\ 1.5 \end{pmatrix}
    \right)\right)
    \end{align},
    $$

   where $\sigma$ is an activation function.

3. Repeat the above process for all vertices in the graph, and for multiple iterations until we reach convergence.

There are many variations of the above algorithm, for example, we can apply graph convolutions to update the representations of the vertices  (Kipf & Welling, *Semi-Supervised Classification with Graph Convolutional Networks*, available at http://arxiv.org/abs/1609.02907), or use attention mechanism to aggregate the neighbor information (Veličković et al, *Graph Attention Networks*, available at http://arxiv.org/abs/1710.10903). In any case, the key to GNN message passing algorithm is to capture the information of each vertex and the relationships between them.

A more specific GNN model for forecasting is the StemGNN (Stem Graph Neural Network) model for multivariate time series forecasting. StemGNN first builds a graph for the correlations between the input multivariate time series using a self-attention mechanism, following by graph convolutions before spitting out the backcast and forecast. Note that the **S** in the name StemGNN is for "Spectral", which refers to the fact that graph convolution is performed in the Fourier domain. As of writing, StemGNN is already included in the `neuralforecast` library.


## Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks

Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN) is a new family of neural networks that use superposition of base functions to approximate any continuous functions. For example, if we have a continuous function $f(x_{p=1}, x_{p=2})$ of two variales $x_{p=1}$ and $x_{p=2}$, the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem states that there exists a decomposition

$$
\begin{align}
&f(x_{p=1}, x_{p=2}) \\
=& \sum_{q=1}^{5} \Phi_{q} \left( \phi_{q,p=1}(x_{p=1}) + \phi_{q,p=2}(x_{p=2}) \right) \\
=&\sum_{q=1}^{2n+1} \Phi_{q} \left(\sum_{p=1}^{n} \phi_{q, p} (x_{p}) \right),
\end{align}
$$

where $n=2$ as we have two variables. We require that the domain of $\phi_{q,p}$ to be $\left[0, 1\right]$, such as, the famous B-spline $B$, a shifted Legendre polynomial $\tilde P_n(x)$. Note that Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem works for more than two variables, and we only choose two variables for simplicity.

The KAN model is constructed using a recursive structure. First, we obtain the sum $\sum_{p=1}^{n} \phi_{q, p} (x_{p})$ for $q=1$, as shown in the computational graph in @fig-kan-structure-q-1.

![Computational graph of the $q=1$ component of a KAN model.](images/chap10_images/kan-illustration-single-layer.png){#fig-kan-structure-q-1 width=90%}

Mathematically, the $q=1$ component is written in the top circle of @fig-kan-structure-q-1. As @fig-kan-structure-q-1 is tedious to draw and read, we simplify it into @fig-kan-structure-q-1-simplify.

![Simplified computational graph of the $q=1$ component of a KAN model.](images/chap10_images/kan-illustration-single-layer-simplify.png){#fig-kan-structure-q-1-simplify width=90%}

We can use the output $x^{L=2}_{p=1}$ from the first layer $L=1$ as the input for the next layer $L=2$. However, before we move on to build a second layer, we need to finish our layer $L=1$ first. We add a second output from layer 1 in @fig-kan-structure-multilayer. Note that we just need to repeat five times to get all our outputs for the first layer. Using the five outputs from the first layer, we can build the second layer, also shown in @fig-kan-structure-multilayer.

![Computational graph of the first layer of a KAN model.](images/chap10_images/kan-illustration-multiple.png){#fig-kan-structure-multilayer width=100%}

Training a KAN model is usually slower than a MLP with comparable amount of parameters. However, KAN can be used to estimated more complicated patterns with the same amount of parameters. Similar to other models mentioned above, KAN is also included in the `neuralforecast` library by Nixtla.


## Foundation Models

Foundation models such as **LLM**s, are taking the tech world by storm. A pre-trained large language model can be used to perform a variety of language-related zero-shot tasks. Similarly, a pre-trained large time series forecasting model can perform zero-shot forecasting tasks, i.e., forecasting without any model training.

At the time of writing, there are a few time series foundation models. We will briefly discuss three types of them: Language model adapted for time series forecasting, models pretrained using time series data, and a special model called TabPFN that is pretrained with tabular data.

LLMs are trained on vast amounts of text data, learning to predict the next word in a sentence. The same concept inspired people working on time series forecasting. In fact, the first approaches were to use LLM as the time series foundation model. However, reusing LLM for time series forecasting requires us to answer questions such as how the time series data is encoded in a LLM. Some methods, such as Time-LLM (M. Jin et al., *Time-LLM: Time series forecasting by reprogramming large language models*, available at: http://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01728), use reprogramming, e.g., aligning time series data with text data using a small network so that the time series data is translated into language data. 


On the other hand, language models are specialized in language tasks. Considering the fact that time series data is also sequential just like natural language, we can directly pre-trained a model from scratch using time series data. Time-GPT was the first model of its kind, pre-trained on time series data, and it is based on the GPT architecture. While some technical details are missing, Time-GPT is a vanilla transformer model, trained on a bunch of diverse datasets with different frequencies and different forecast horizons. Since Time-GPT is not open source, we will focus more on an open-source time series foundation model called Lag-Llama.

To get started with the core concept of the Lag-llama model, we come back to our mental model of a swing. A swing oscillates but the amplitude diminishes. The time series will show this clearly. However, there is a different perspective to visualize and capture the idea. We plot out our swing angle at time $t$ against the swing angle at time $t-1$. The plot will show a pattern that the swing angle is oscillating but becoming smaller, as shown in @fig-ts-foundation-model-swing-angle-dyn. This diagram is called a phase space diagram, and it captures the dynamics of the time series data.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-ts-foundation-model-swing-angle-dyn
#| fig-cap: "Angle of a swing comparing to its previous time step. The swing starts from the top right of this so-called phase space diagram. The pattern indicates that the swing angle is oscillating but becoming smaller."
df_swing_angle = pd.read_csv("data/chapter10/swing_angle_ts.csv")

_, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 7))

df_swing_angle.plot(
    x="theta",
    y="theta_1",
    ax=ax,
    legend=False
)

ax.set_xlabel(rf"$\theta(t)$")
ax.set_ylabel(rf"$\theta(t-1)$")
ax.set_title("Swing Angle Dynamics");
```

Lag-Llama is based on the idea that a phase space of the time series captures the dynamics of the time series data. The input of the Lag-Llama model is original time series with different lags. For example, given a time series
$\cdots, 1, 2, 3, 4$, we convert it into the following input by lagging it by 1:

$$
\text{Input} = \begin{pmatrix}
1 & 2 \\
2 & 3 \\
3 & 4
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The first column represents the original data, while the second column lags by 1, and we can add more columns by lagging more.

Each row is a point in a high-dimensional phase space similar to the one we have in @fig-ts-foundation-model-swing-angle-dyn. The core model, as the name indicates, is a Llama architecture. Now we have the data input and model architecture, we can train it on a diverse set of data. After training, Lag-Llama can be used as a zero shot model for time series forecasting.

The third category of foundation models, as we mentioned earlier, is TabPFN. TabPFN is a model that is pretrained on tabular data. Similar to other foundation models, TabPFN is also a transformer-based model. However, TabPFN utilizes an attention mechanism that helps the model to capture both column-wise and row-wise relationships in the tabular data. Thus it is useful in time series forecasting tasks too. Normally, we have the train-evaluate-test paradigm for each forecasting problem we are solving, where we understand the forecasting problem, build a model, train and evaluate using a dataset, and finally perform out of sample tests using a holdout dataset. TabPFN dropped the paradigm, and it uses the so-called In-Context-Learning (ICL) for zero shot forecasting. In ICL, the model recieves the input data and the task together and makes predictions based on all the input without additional training. Similar to LLMs, TabPFN is a pretrained model. TabPFN is a good candidate for time series forecasting on small datasets. We encourage the reader to check out the original paper by N. Hollmann et al., “Accurate predictions on small data with a tabular foundation model,” available at https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-08328-6.


## Summary

In this chapter, we discussed several neural network models for time series forecasting. We will not dive deep into these models, however, we recommend the reader to at least understand the basic concepts of these models. Time series forecasting is a complicated task, and different domains and different datasets require different models. With more intuitions of different models, the reader can better choose our model for the task at hand. We also discussed several foundation models, which are pretrained models that can be used for zero-shot forecasting tasks. These models are useful when we want to quickly perform a forecasting task or as baselines for our models if we have no financial constraints.
